Apache Knox: topology authentication and service ACLs need separate review


Apache Knox is a gateway in front of Hadoop and related services. It can terminate authentication, assert an identity to a backend, apply service-level ACLs, and expose an administrative API. When it is exposed, the gateway's topology becomes part of the security boundary. A request may be authenticated at Knox, authorized by a Knox ACL, and then authorized again by the service behind it.
On 2026-11-08, ZoomEye count-only probes returned 0 matches for app="Apache Knox", 0 for title="Apache Knox", and 921 for http.body="Apache Knox". The query used sub_type=all, page 1, and page size 1. The absence of app and title matches is a fingerprint limitation, not evidence that no Knox gateways are deployed. The body count …

articles.author: Mirosław Adamczewski
articles.description:
A Simple Boundary Value Analysis Exercise for Beginner QA Testers
One of the easiest ways to understand Boundary Value Analysis is to stop reading about it and test an actual rule.
Imagine this requirement:
Free delivery applies to orders of $50.00 or more. Orders below $50.00 cost $4.99 to deliver.
What values would you test?
A useful starting point is:
$49.99
$50.00
$50.01
The interesting part is not only executing those three cases.
Before testing, try to define:
the expected result for each value,
which value is the exact boundary,
what behaviour would count as a defect,
what evidence you would capture,
how you would document the issue if something went wrong.
That small exercise already combines several useful QA skills:
requirement analysis → test design → execution → expected vs actual → evidence → bug reporting
I turned it into a free worksheet for people learning manual software testing.
It includes:
the requirement,
a short BVA explanation,
a test worksheet,
bug report fields,
reflection questions.
There is deliberately no solution included — the point is to make your own prediction before checking the behaviour.
You can get the exercise for free here:
👉 https://qapracticekit.com/learn/free-boundary-value-analysis-exercise/
No payment or credit card required.
If you're learning QA, I'd also be interested to hear: which testing technique was the hardest for you to understand before you started practising it?


  
  
  testing #qa #beginners #softwaretesting
articles.title: A Simple Boundary Value Analysis Exercise for Beginner QA Testers

articles.author: zhitong
articles.description:
In the spring of 2004, 41-year-old Andy Rubin stared at an eviction notice on the door of his Palo Alto office. Ousted from his previous startup Danger and rejected by every VC on Sand Hill Road for his "operating system for digital cameras," Rubin was completely out of cash—surviving only because his friend Steve Perlman handed him $10,000 in cash from an ATM.
Three years later, that broke 41-year-old engineer used a radical product distribution weapon—giving away a modern mobile OS for $0—to put Android into 3.5 billion active devices and capture 71% of the global smartphone market.

Rubin realized handset giants like Samsung, Motorola, and HTC were trapped between Microsoft's $15–$25/unit Windows Mobile licensing fee and Nokia's Symbian stronghold. Acquired by Google for $50M in 2005, Rubin built the open Linux-based platform the entire hardware ecosystem desperately needed.
Watching Steve Jobs unveil the capacitive multi-touch iPhone from a taxi at CES 2007, Rubin ordered the driver to pull over. He immediately scrapped Android's BlackBerry-style keyboard prototype ("Sooner") and rebuilt the OS around full-screen touch and the iconic pull-down notification shade.

By releasing AOSP for free under Apache 2.0 while monetizing via Google Mobile Services (Search, Maps, Play Store), Rubin turned every hardware manufacturer on earth into Google's distribution army—proving that open ecosystems can scale faster than any single vertically integrated giant.
articles.title: PM Rank #54 · Andy Rubin (86 OVR): Evicted and Broke at 41, He Gave Away His OS for Free and Put It in 3.5 Billion Pockets

articles.description:
A rate-limited alert destination is not a reason to retry every failed request. In a healthtech incident, the useful record is the smallest set of events that lets an engineer reconstruct what happened: the source failure, the delivery attempt, the quota response, and the final disposition. Retrying blindly can turn one patient-impacting symptom into a burst of duplicate notifications and a noisier audit trail.
Short answer: treat HTTP 429 as a scheduling signal, honor Retry-After when it is valid, apply exponential backoff with jitter when it is absent, cap the number and age of attempts, and write one structured event for every attempt. Preserve the original alert identity across retries. The alert can be delayed; its evidence must not be rewritten.
Start with identity.
Then preserve tim…
